text:
Build me a Langfuse-style observability dashboard from my own AI coding sessions for the last 7 days.

SOURCES (read locally, read-only):
- Claude Code: ~/.claude/projects/**/*.jsonl
- Codex: ~/.codex/sessions/**/*.jsonl (and ~/.codex/history.jsonl)
Never print secrets, keys or full prompt text. Snippets max 10 words, with keys, paths, URLs and long ids stripped.

STEP 1. Write a stdlib-only Python script that computes, per tool:
- sessions per day, user prompts, tool calls by tool name, failed tool calls by tool and error type
- models used, tokens (input, output, cache read/write) per model per day
- tool-call latency p50/p95, overall and per tool; session length p50/p95
- top sessions by tokens, longest sessions, retries (same tool call repeated after an error)
- prompts clustered into task types (build, debug, deploy, research, writing, UI, review, other)
- sessions grouped by project (working directory), with subagent runs flagged
If a log doesn't record something, write "not logged". Never invent numbers.
Save the result as harness-summary.json.

STEP 2. Render a single-file dashboard.html (dark, animated numbers and charts):
- Summary strip: total tool calls, prompts, error rate, tokens, p95 latency
- Traces table: one row per session (tool, project, start, duration, prompts, tool calls, errors, tokens, model); search, filter by tool, sort, toggle to hide subagent runs
- Trace detail: click a session to see a waterfall of its turns and tool calls with ok/error and duration
- Sessions by project, tokens over time by model, a model table (tokens, error rate)
- Latency view per tool, and an error explorer grouped by tool and error type
- Heuristic scores (tool success rate, retries, per-session health), clearly labeled "heuristic"
Cap embedded traces at the top 200 sessions by tokens if the file gets too big.

STEP 3. From the data, write HARNESS.md proposing changes to CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md:
- Model routing: which model for which task type, based on what I used and what failed
- Tools: keep (high use, low failure), fix (high failure), cut (rarely used)
- Skills: one for every task type I repeated 3+ times, with a trigger line and steps
- Guardrails: my top 3 failure patterns and a check that prevents each
- Budget: my top 5 token sinks and one change that would cut each
Cite the sessions behind each suggestion.

STEP 4. Show me the 5 headline numbers and the proposed diff before changing any config. I'll review weekly and change only what the data shows.
author: Charles
label: long
rationale: Build an observability dashboard from local session logs.

You are lead engineer for Cauldron (also called Workbench). PLAN.md in the repo root is the single source of truth. Read it fully before doing anything. If this prompt and PLAN.md disagree, PLAN.md wins and you tell me.

Scope: Cauldron only. Do not build, reference or integrate Meadow. Do not invent features. If something is missing from section 5 of PLAN.md, ask.

Rules: 

* Token discipline: follow the cost ladder in PLAN.md section 3. Do not re-read files you already read, work from diffs, keep summaries short, and report tokens and frontier calls per milestone.
* Verification: a feature "works" only with a passing test. Write failing acceptance tests first.
* Never weaken, skip or delete a test to get green. Sealed tests are read-only.
* Never use herdr agent state as a gate. Use it only behind the adapter, version pinned.
* Never say "done" without pasting full suite output.
* If blocked, stop and ask. Do not mock around a blocker.


Start: 

1. Read PLAN.md.
2. Do M0 only: the audit table (feature | works/partial/missing/unknown | evidence), plus a list of unresolved TODOs and open questions from PLAN.md that block you (feature list, language, herdr release).
3. Stop and wait for my approval before M1.


Each milestone after that: failing tests, implement, full suite, then a report of at most 15 lines (test counts, tokens, frontier calls, what is left), then commit.
Stop for my review after M2, M5, M8 and M10. Otherwise continue to the next milestone.

text:
You are the lead engineer for Cauldron (also called Workbench).
I'm attaching Cauldron_M0_Revised_Audit.md. This document contains the revisions I expect to the initial M0 audit.
Your task is to produce the final, evidence-backed M0 audit. Do not start M1 or implement anything.
1. Read and establish the baseline
Read:

* `PLAN.md` in the repository root — the single source of truth.
* The attached `Cauldron_M0_Revised_Audit.md` — the requested audit corrections.
* The current repository state and relevant source files/tests.

If the attached audit conflicts with `PLAN.md`, `PLAN.md` wins. If either document makes a claim unsupported by the repository, investigate and correct it.
2. Critical architectural requirement: frontier efficiency
This is one of Cauldron's defining requirements, not a secondary optimization.
Do not describe the existing implementation as satisfying this architecture simply because local model routing or cheap-first worker execution exists.
Independently audit these capabilities:

* Cheap-first execution routing.
* Local decision model selection.
* Local task classification and confidence scoring.
* Frontier-only-when-needed orchestration.
* Cost-aware escalation.
* Single frontier escalation with a compact failure digest.
* Bounded local executor architecture.
* Human handoff after failed escalation.

Distinguish existing primitives from verified end-to-end capabilities. Explicitly identify what works, what is partial, and what is missing.
The objective is to build a system that is local-first in its decision-making and execution, using frontier models only when genuinely necessary, while minimizing total cost-to-green.
3. Complete the audit
Review the entire plan, particularly sections 5–11.
For every feature and acceptance requirement, provide:
`Feature | Status (works/partial/missing/unknown) | Evidence`
Rules:

* Works requires a passing test proving the required behavior.
* Related infrastructure does not prove the complete feature works.
* Partial must identify exactly what exists and what is missing.
* Unknown means code exists but evidence is insufficient.
* Missing means no implementation was found.
* Do not infer functionality from module names or documentation alone.

Preserve the distinction between existing infrastructure, required Cauldron functionality, and unrelated existing capabilities.
Pay particular attention to:

* Planning checklist and baseline capture.
* Builder/Rampart separation and sealed tests.
* Flake checks, mutation testing and traceability.
* All three gates.
* Escalation policy and loop limits.
* Memory security, provenance and evaluation.
* Model, skill and plugin allowlists.
* Regression testing in ADE and IDE modes.
* Section 3.4 metrics.
* Recorded trace replay.

4. Decisions and blockers
Apply requirements already established in `PLAN.md` without asking me to reconfirm them.
Do not select a decision model before the evaluation required by section 10.
Keep the herdr release question scoped to M6.
Leave unrelated existing features untouched unless their inclusion in Cauldron is explicitly confirmed.
Do not silently decide the implementation language. Present the Rust recommendation and its trade-offs against TypeScript and Go.
Separate genuine M0 blockers from questions that only block later milestones.
5. Final deliverable
Return:

1. The complete revised audit table.
2. A section-by-section acceptance coverage matrix.
3. A list of verified existing capabilities and their limitations.
4. A list of missing critical architectural capabilities, especially frontier-efficient orchestration.
5. Remaining TODOs and decisions, classified by the milestone they block.
6. Repository commit and test-suite baseline, including exclusions.
7. Token usage and frontier calls, reporting unavailable measurements honestly.

Do not modify product code, create implementation commits, start M1, or work around missing evidence.
M0 is not approved until I review the final audit and explicitly authorize M1.
Stop after delivering the audit.
Evidence standard
Every audit claim must be traceable to verifiable repository evidence.
Use this hierarchy:

1. Passing automated test: strongest evidence. Include the exact test name and test command.
2. Source-code evidence: identify the exact file, function or symbol, and relevant line numbers. Source code alone does not qualify a feature as working.
3. Runtime evidence: provide reproducible command output or execution traces demonstrating the behavior.
4. Documentation or comments: supporting context only, never proof of implementation.

Additional rules:

* Every `works` classification requires a passing test exercising the actual acceptance criterion.
* A test passing without exercising the required behavior is insufficient.
* Distinguish unit tests, integration tests and end-to-end tests.
* Report unexecuted, excluded, skipped and failing tests explicitly.
* Never invent test names, execution results, file locations or line numbers.
* If evidence cannot be independently verified, classify the requirement as `unknown`, not `works`.
* For partial implementations, provide separate evidence for what exists and explicitly identify what remains unproven.

Audit principle: no claim without evidence, no feature marked working without a passing behavioral test.

text:
M1 review: the implementation and tests establish a good foundation, but I don't want to close M1 until we resolve several remaining policy and budget guarantees.
Please do a focused M1 review and hardening pass.
1. Policy defaults
The current implicit-open behaviour is too permissive.
Propose a migration-compatible policy:

* New projects receive explicit allowlists by default.
* Existing configurations can retain legacy-open behaviour through an explicit compatibility mode.
* Missing policy configuration produces a visible warning.
* An explicitly empty list continues to deny everything.

Do not silently break existing projects. Show the migration proposal before changing behaviour.
2. Budget correctness
The `ceil(chars / 3)` input-token estimate is a heuristic and does not establish a hard budget guarantee.
Investigate:

* Model/provider-specific token counting.
* A conservative fallback with a documented safety margin.
* Atomic pre-call budget reservations across concurrent agents.
* Maximum output-cost reservation and reconciliation against actual usage.
* Refusal when the remaining budget cannot safely cover a call.

Add tests for Unicode, source code, long tool schemas and concurrent calls. Do not claim hard enforcement if the estimator still permits unbounded overspend.
3. Policy-file integrity
Bash can still modify `backspace.toml`, potentially changing the policy loaded by the next session.
Prevent agents from modifying the authoritative policy file, independently of the file-tool restrictions. Prefer a host-controlled, read-only policy source or another enforceable integrity boundary.
Add a test showing that an agent cannot weaken policy for a subsequent session.
4. Budget coverage
Review every provider and CLI execution path.
In particular:

* CLI workers must not bypass hard task budgets.
* Advisor and cloud-chat paths must have an explicit documented budget boundary.
* No task-scoped model call should bypass the gateway silently.

Plugin E2E coverage can remain assigned to M11 because there is no plugin loader yet, but keep the current gateway-level evidence classified accurately.
5. Deliverables

* List the actual gaps and proposed fixes before implementation.
* Write failing acceptance tests first.
* Preserve all existing tests; do not weaken them.
* Keep each change within M1 scope.
* Provide exact red and green commit hashes, full suite output, changed-file diff, and measured token/frontier-call information where available.

Do not start M2 or M3 implementation during this pass. M1 remains pending review until I approve the final result.

Scope

3. The `max_project_tokens` configuration change and its operational implications.

Do not start M2 or M3. Do not expand this task into M6 sandboxing, plugin loading, real-provider spend tests, or general refactoring.
1. JevRouter: reservation settlement and strict-budget behaviour
The current documentation says JevRouter reserves against the project dollar budget before making a call, assumes a 512-token answer, and records the actual cost after the response. Router tokens are not counted against `max_project_tokens`.
Verify the implementation and answer these questions:

* Is the reservation held for the entire period in which Jev can incur cost?
* Is there a window between releasing the reservation and recording actual spend?
* Can multiple concurrent Jev calls complete close together and allow another API reservation to pass before their actual costs are recorded?
* Can an API reservation or another Jev call observe an inconsistent combination of held reservations and recorded spend?
* Is actual cost above the reservation recorded before the reserved amount becomes available to other calls?

If there is a race, fix it using the smallest correct change. Prefer an atomic reservation-to-actual-spend settlement, or an equivalent approach under the same synchronization mechanism. Do not merely add a test that confirms the current behaviour.
Required tests
Add concurrency tests that exercise:

* Multiple simultaneous JevRouter calls against one project budget.
* Jev calls completing while another API reservation attempts to use the same budget.
* Actual cost exceeding the estimate, where applicable.
* Reservation release and spend settlement without a gap in which another call can incorrectly use the budget.

The tests must demonstrate the invariant, not just that the calls complete successfully.
Strict-budget behaviour
A 512-token Jev answer is an estimate, not a provider-enforced output cap. Therefore, JevRouter is not currently a fully bounded path for strict-budget tasks.
Determine whether the existing configuration and policy model provides a reliable way to bypass JevRouter for a strict task.

* If there is already a supported mechanism, use it and add tests proving Jev is not called and the heuristic is used instead.
* If there is no such mechanism, do not invent an implicit strict mode. Make the limitation explicit in `M1-BUDGET-BOUNDARIES.md`: strict-budget tasks must bypass JevRouter operationally, and the current system does not enforce that requirement automatically.
* Do not describe JevRouter as a fully guaranteed strict-budget path.

Keep the distinction between project-dollar reservations and project-token limits explicit.
2. Project-policy coverage: audit every model-call path
The current budget table does not make project-policy coverage sufficiently explicit.
Trace every model-call path in the codebase. At minimum inspect:

* API agent turns through `drive`.
* CLI workers through `finish_cli`.
* CLI planners through `plan_on_cli`.
* Anthropic's server-side advisor tool.
* Claude Code's own advisor and scout subagents.
* JevRouter.
* CloudChatServer.
* AgentChat, including CLI, local-model and router-backed conversations.
* Remote harnesses.
* Plugin call sites, including the current pre-loader gateway checks.

For each path, verify what actually happens. Do not infer policy enforcement from budget enforcement, or vice versa.
Update `M1-BUDGET-BOUNDARIES.md` with a distinct Project policy check column. Use precise descriptions such as:

* Checked against the relevant project orchestration/execution allowlist.
* Checked by the CLI's own configuration, not independently by the gateway.
* Not covered by the project's policy.
* Runs under the remote machine's own policy.
* Gateway-level check only; no end-to-end loader exists yet.

Where a path has separate orchestration and execution roles, state which role is checked.
Also inspect whether CLI workers, CLI planners and JevRouter can select or invoke models that bypass the intended project allowlists. If you find a real bypass, fix it and add a regression test. Do not claim coverage merely because an API call elsewhere uses the gateway.
The result must let a reader answer two independent questions for every path:

1. Does the project's budget cover it, and how?
2. Does the project's model policy cover it, and how?

3. `max_project_tokens`: confirm the configuration decision
The second hardening round introduced `[orchestrator] max_project_tokens` next to `max_project_usd`.
This enables multiple CLI workers to contend for a shared token budget, but it also means:

* CLI turns sharing the project token budget run one at a time.
* A CLI turn holds the remaining allowance while it runs.
* API calls sharing that budget are refused rather than queued during the CLI hold.
* A CLI turn can still overshoot according to the documented CLI reporting limitations.

Do not silently remove or redesign this mechanism.
Verify:

* The config field is parsed, persisted and applied at the correct project scope.
* Existing configs without this field remain backward-compatible.
* The limit is included in the relevant CLI and API admission/reservation checks.
* The concurrency tests actually exercise a shared project-level token scope.
* Documentation and examples describe the serialization and refusal behaviour accurately.

In the final report, state the implications of keeping this as a supported configuration knob. Do not introduce a per-turn allowance such as `cli_turn_tokens` in this pass.
4. Documentation and wording
Update `M1-BUDGET-BOUNDARIES.md` and `M1-HARDENING-NOTES.md` to agree with the implementation and test evidence.
Preserve the existing terminology:

* reserved
* admitted
* unmetered

Do not call any path a hard budget guarantee.
Keep all previously documented assumptions and limitations:

* Plugin loader not implemented until M11.

Make a clear distinction between:

text:
# MASTER PROMPT — M1 FINAL HARDENING AND SIGN-OFF

You are continuing the M1 hardening work on Cauldron / Workbench.

Your objective is to bring M1 to a state where it can be reviewed and explicitly approved by the project owner.

This is a closure pass, not a new implementation phase. Fix the remaining correctness, policy, accounting, testing and documentation gaps. Preserve the work already completed.

**M1 is not approved. Do not approve it yourself.**

## 0. Establish the current state first

Before modifying anything:

1. Inspect the current branch, `git status`, recent commits and uncommitted changes.
2. Confirm that the third-review green commit `b2a73af0c8110225032fdb4b5402804a0cbdba75` is present in the history, or identify the actual equivalent current baseline.
3. Read:
   - `PLAN.md`
   - `M1-BUDGET-BOUNDARIES.md`
   - `M1-HARDENING-NOTES.md`
   - Relevant implementation and test files.
4. Verify the current behaviour directly. Do not rely exclusively on previous reports.
5. Identify any work already completed after the third-review report. Do not duplicate it.

Baseline evidence from the previous report:
- Red commit: `5cdd77ddeb4c80ed31e289126f799d90f4ffe4a8`
- Green commit: `b2a73af0c8110225032fdb4b5402804a0cbdba75`
- 429 tests passed in the reported green run.
- No real provider, CLI or Jev was called.
- M1 remained pending.

Preserve existing work unless there is a demonstrated correctness problem.

## 1. Decisions for this pass

Use these decisions as the default design direction. Do not leave them implicit or silently defer them.

### Decision A — Keep `max_project_tokens`

Retain `[orchestrator] max_project_tokens`.

It provides a shared project-level token scope for API reservations and CLI admissions. Accept the current trade-offs:

- CLI turns sharing the budget run one at a time.
- An API call using that budget is refused while a CLI turn holds the allowance.
- The API call is not queued.
- Claude Code can overshoot within one reported turn.
- JevRouter does not count against this project token limit.

Do not introduce `cli_turn_tokens` in this pass.

### Decision B — Keep advisor and scout gating fail-closed

Under an enforced project policy:

- Claude Code's `--advisor` must only be passed if its configured model is explicitly allowed for the relevant role.
- Claude Code's scout model passed through `--agents` must only be passed if explicitly allowed for execution.
- If the model is not allowed, leave the feature off and record a clear log message.
- Generated policies may explicitly include the existing intended aliases (`opus` and `haiku`) in their appropriate lists.
- Handwritten enforced policies must never be silently widened.

Retain tests proving that removing the relevant policy check causes a failure.

### Decision C — Jev's own model must be explicitly governed

Do not silently treat Jev's own model as an unrestricted trusted exception.

Use an explicit routing-model policy entry, separate from ordinary orchestration and execution roles, if the current policy structure does not already provide an equivalent mechanism.

Requirements:

- Enforced policies must explicitly permit the configured Jev model.
- Generated new-project policies should name the intended configured routing model.
- Legacy configurations should preserve their documented compatibility and warning behaviour.
- Do not widen orchestration or execution lists merely to make Jev pass.
- If Jev's model is not allowed, do not call it; use the deterministic heuristic instead.
- Test both permitted and refused routing calls.

Keep the distinction between the router's own classification model and the candidate models it may select.

### Decision D — M1 does not claim OS-level security

Accept the policy restore guard as a limited M1 protection mechanism.

Do not claim it is a security boundary against determined processes running under the same operating-system user.

M6 sandboxing or an equivalent separate OS-user boundary remains necessary for that stronger guarantee.

## 2. JevRouter — close the unknown-cost failure case

The third review established an atomic settlement invariant for successful Jev responses:

The reservation and actual spend must never both be absent between dispatch and settlement. Recording actual spend and releasing the hold happen under the same reservation lock.

However, one case remains unresolved:

**A Jev request can be dispatched and then fail without returning usable usage or billing information. Its actual cost is unknown.**

Do not release its reservation as though the request had never happened.

### Required behaviour

Distinguish at least these cases:

1. **Failure before dispatch**

   No request was sent. The reservation can be released.

2. **Successful response with known cost**

   Record the actual cost, including any amount above the reservation, then release the reservation atomically.

3. **Failure after dispatch with unknown cost**

   Do not silently free the reservation. Conservatively retain or account for the reserved amount as unknown-cost spend against the relevant project budget. Record the uncertainty explicitly.

4. **Failure after dispatch with known cost**

   Record the known cost and settle atomically, even if the response cannot be used for classification.

The unknown-cost state must not be counted twice, silently forgotten, or made available to another request simply because an exception occurred.

If existing accounting is persisted, ensure unknown-cost accounting follows the same persistence guarantees. If accounting is process-local, document that boundary explicitly.

### Required tests

Add tests for:

- Failure before dispatch releases the reservation.
- Timeout after dispatch does not release it as zero spend.
- Connection interruption after dispatch retains conservative accounting.
- Response parsing failure after dispatch is handled correctly.
- A later request cannot consume the retained reservation.
- A retry does not accidentally free or double-count the previous attempt.
- Concurrent Jev requests with a mixture of successful, failed and unknown-cost outcomes.
- A concurrent API reservation attempting to use the same project budget during settlement.
- Known actual cost exceeding the reservation is recorded in full.
- The heuristic fallback still operates when a Jev request is refused or fails.

Use mocks and deterministic synchronization. Do not call real Jev.

The invariant must be tested at the reservation/accounting level, not inferred from log messages.

### Settlement mutation test

Retain a mutation check that demonstrates why atomic settlement matters.

Where practical, deliberately change the implementation to release first and record afterwards. At least one test must fail because it detects the reservation gap.

## 3. Enforce actual model policy at CLI boundaries

The current policy matrix distinguishes CLI entry checks from the underlying model selected by Claude Code or Codex.

That distinction must not be obscured.

A policy allowing the executable `claude` does not automatically prove that a particular model selected internally by Claude Code is allowed.

Audit the actual invocation paths for:

- CLI workers through `finish_cli`.
- CLI planners through `plan_on_cli`.
- Claude Code's model selection.
- Codex model selection.
- Claude Code's `--advisor`.
- Claude Code's scout model passed through `--agents`.
- Environment variables, personal CLI configuration and project configuration that can change model selection.

### Required behaviour under enforced policy

The project must not claim model-level enforcement where it only checks the CLI executable.

For each CLI:

1. Determine whether the selected model can be reliably identified or explicitly pinned through the invocation.
2. If it can, ensure the selected model is checked against the relevant project allowlist.
3. Prevent untrusted project or agent input from changing that selection after validation.
4. If the model cannot be reliably identified or pinned, fail closed under an enforced policy unless an explicit documented policy exception exists.
5. Do not make assumptions about CLI flags. Verify the actual supported invocation behaviour in the current implementation and tests.

Do not weaken legacy compatibility. Existing legacy/open configurations should continue according to the documented warning behaviour.

### Tests

Test:
- Allowed CLI executable and allowed underlying model.
- Allowed CLI executable but disallowed underlying model.
- Missing or ambiguous underlying model under enforced policy.
- Attempts to override model selection through environment/configuration where applicable.
- Planner and worker roles separately.
- Advisor and scout aliases separately.
- Legacy policy behaviour.

If real CLI behaviour cannot be verified in this environment, state that limitation. Fake CLI tests prove what Backspace passes, not how the real CLI interprets it.

## 4. JevRouter — strict-budget and token-budget semantics

Keep the existing supported project-wide heuristic bypass:

`[router] backend = "heuristic"`

Verify that it prevents Jev from being called.

Do not describe a router pin as a Jev bypass. Verify the current behaviour and retain the regression test.

Do not invent a per-task strict mode in this pass unless a real requirement already exists in `PLAN.md`.

Document the exact distinction:

- A project using the heuristic backend can avoid Jev.
- The system does not currently enforce this choice specifically for individual strict-budget tasks.
- Jev's assumed output size is not provider-capped.
- Jev's own classification call is governed by the explicit routing-model policy.
- Jev reservations count against the project dollar budget when one exists.
- Jev tokens do not count toward `max_project_tokens`.
- A router without a project budget remains unmetered.

Ensure that the budget table and strict-budget section say the same thing.

## 5. Re-audit the entire project policy and budget matrix

For every model-call path, answer two separate questions:

1. How does the project budget cover this call?
2. How does project policy govern this call?

The table must include at least:

- API agent turns through `drive`.
- API advisors.
- CLI workers.
- CLI planners.
- Claude Code advisors.
- Claude Code scouts.
- JevRouter's own model.
- JevRouter's candidate models.
- CloudChatServer.
- AgentChat, including CLI, local model, router and Backspace Cloud paths.
- Remote harnesses.
- Plugins.

Use distinct columns:

| Path | Budget classification and enforcement | Project policy check | Remaining limitation |
|---|---|---|---|

Preserve the terminology:

- `reserved`
- `admitted`
- `unmetered`
- `out of this process`

Do not suggest that budget enforcement implies policy enforcement or vice versa.

The table must identify whether a path is:
- Checked against orchestration policy.
- Checked against execution policy.
- Checked against a dedicated routing-model policy.
- Governed only by the CLI's own configuration.
- Not covered by project policy.
- Governed by the remote machine's policy.
- Covered only by gateway-level tests without an actual call site.

No row should leave the reader guessing.

## 6. Reconfirm `max_project_tokens`

Retain the configuration and verify it end to end.

Acceptance criteria:

- Optional whole-number configuration under `[orchestrator]`.
- Older configurations without it still load.
- The field survives configuration write-back.
- The shipped example documents it.
- API reservations and CLI admissions share the project token scope.
- Concurrent CLI turns cannot receive the same remaining allowance.
- Concurrent API reservations cannot jointly exceed the shared token limit under the documented assumptions.
- API calls are refused rather than queued while a CLI turn holds the shared allowance.
- JevRouter is excluded from project token counting and this exclusion is explicit.
- CLI dollar-budget refusal remains fail-closed.
- Existing projects without the setting are unaffected.

Do not implement a per-turn token allocation in this pass.

## 7. Revalidate advisor and scout policy generation

Verify both generated new-project configuration and handwritten policy behaviour.

Acceptance criteria:

- Generated policies explicitly contain the intended advisor and scout aliases.
- Advisor alias is listed in the correct role.
- Scout alias is listed in the correct role.
- Handwritten enforced lists are never automatically widened.
- Missing aliases result in the associated feature being omitted.
- Logs explain why the feature was omitted.
- Policy adoption remains a human-reviewed operation.

Also verify the newly introduced routing-model policy entry and its default-generation behaviour.

## 8. Audit policy-integrity limitations

Do not expand this into M6.

Verify the current guard still:
- Loads the authoritative policy lock.
- Refuses unreadable or invalid policy state rather than silently falling back.
- Detects and restores covered modifications after tool batches and CLI turns.
- Prevents unapproved policy adoption.
- Requires human approval for changes to project policy.

Retain the explicit limitation that a long-running process may modify files between monitored actions, and that this is not an OS security boundary.

Do not rewrite the documentation to imply otherwise.

## 9. Resolve the two flaky tests

The previous third-review report identified two timing flakes in untouched tests:

- `spec_gate::the_gate_refuses_twice_then_opens`
- `webhook::a_webhook_wakes_only_its_bot`

Investigate both independently.

Required steps:

1. Run each test repeatedly in isolation.
2. Run them under the full suite.
3. Determine whether each failure is a test-timing issue, shared-state interference or an actual product defect.
4. Capture reproducible failure evidence where possible.
5. Make the smallest safe correction if the issue is genuinely test-only.
6. Do not change webhook product behaviour merely to make a flaky test pass.
7. If a product-level webhook fix is required, do not silently implement it as unrelated M1 work. Clearly report the finding and keep it separate for owner approval.

Run repeated full-suite checks after any correction.

A single passing run is not sufficient evidence of stability.

## 10. Documentation must match the implementation

Update:

- `M1-BUDGET-BOUNDARIES.md`
- `M1-HARDENING-NOTES.md`

Update only the necessary sections of `PLAN.md`, if a confirmed M1 requirement demands it. Do not modify unrelated roadmap or milestone content.

Keep explicit descriptions of:

- API byte-per-token assumption.
- Provider overhead allowance.
- Configured pricing accuracy.
- Provider enforcement of `max_tokens`.
- Advisor output being unbounded by a provider-side output cap.
- Jev output assumption.
- Unknown-cost Jev request handling.
- Claude Code end-of-turn usage reporting.
- Codex cumulative-versus-per-turn semantics being unverified.
- CLI policy versus CLI model-selection enforcement.
- Unmetered CloudChatServer and AgentChat.
- Remote harnesses using their own policy and budgets.
- `max_project_tokens` serialization and refusal trade-offs.
- Router exclusion from project token counting.
- Policy restore guard not being OS-level security.
- Plugin loader not existing until M11.

Use accurate wording. Never claim a hard budget guarantee.

Clearly separate:
1. Implemented and tested controls.
2. Operational recommendations.
3. Assumptions.
4. Known limitations.
5. Future work.

## 11. Test requirements and red/green evidence

For each implementation change:

1. Add a failing test first.
2. Capture the red result.
3. Implement the smallest correct change.
4. Capture the green result.
5. Preserve existing tests.
6. Do not edit old tests simply to pass unless the previous expectation is demonstrably wrong.
7. Explain any test correction.

Run:

`cargo test --no-fail-fast`

Also run targeted test files independently.

Run the complete suite repeatedly, ideally at least five consecutive successful runs after the fixes. If the environment makes that impractical, state exactly how many runs were completed and why.

Report:

- Exact commands.
- Test counts for each run.
- New tests added in this pass.
- Existing tests preserved or corrected.
- Red and green commit hashes.
- Final branch and working-tree status.
- Any crates not built in the environment.
- Any skipped tests.
- Whether tests used real providers, real CLIs or real Jev.
- Whether token consumption was measured.
- Remaining differences between what tests establish and what external services may actually do.

Do not describe fake CLIs as real CLI validation.

Do not describe mocks as provider validation.

## 12. Non-negotiable scope boundaries

Do not:
- Start M2 or M3.
- Implement M6 sandboxing.
- Implement plugin loading.
- Add unrelated product features.
- Make real frontier-model calls.
- Make real Jev calls.
- Make unrelated refactors.
- Weaken existing policy or budget controls.
- Silently widen allowlists.
- Hide test failures.
- Rewrite the roadmap.
- Mark M1 approved.

If you discover a problem outside M1, document it separately rather than absorbing it into this pass.

## 13. Final acceptance criteria

M1 can be recommended for approval only when:

1. Jev settlement is atomic for successful and known-cost outcomes.
2. Post-dispatch unknown-cost failures cannot silently release the reservation as zero spend.
3. Concurrent Jev and API reservations have regression coverage.
4. Jev's own model is governed by an explicit routing-model policy.
5. CLI model-selection limitations are either enforced or clearly fail-closed and documented.
6. Advisor and scout policy checks are covered by tests.
7. The budget and policy matrix covers every known model-call path.
8. `max_project_tokens` is verified and its trade-offs are explicit.
9. The two previously flaky tests have been investigated and classified.
10. All relevant tests pass consistently.
11. Documentation accurately reflects implementation and remaining limitations.
12. No M2 or M3 work has been started.

## 14. Final report format

Return a concise but evidence-rich report with these sections:

### A. Baseline
Current branch, starting commit, working-tree state and existing work discovered.

### B. Findings
Every remaining defect found, with the relevant code path.

### C. Changes
Files changed and exact behaviour altered.

### D. JevRouter
Settlement invariant, unknown-cost handling, concurrency evidence, routing policy and token-budget treatment.

### E. CLI policy
How actual model selection is handled for Claude Code and Codex. Distinguish verified enforcement from assumptions.

### F. Policy and budget matrix
Every path, with separate budget and policy coverage.

### G. `max_project_tokens`
Verified configuration, scope, concurrency, compatibility and trade-offs.

### H. Flaky tests
Reproduction, cause, changes and repeated-run evidence.

### I. Test results
Red/green commits, full-suite results, repeated runs, new test count and external-validation limitations.

### J. Remaining risks
Every limitation that remains, including M6 and real CLI/provider uncertainty.

### K. M1 recommendation
Choose one:
- Recommend approval.
- Keep pending, with exact blockers.

Do not sign off M1 yourself. The project owner makes that decision.

**The objective is not to produce a green test count at any cost. The objective is to make the implementation, policy, budget accounting, tests and documentation tell the same truth.**

text:
Subagents are the biggest cause of AI failures

In most harnesses:
1. Main agent writes a summary of what it knows
2. Subagent starts from that summary only, and makes assumptions
3. Subagent works and sends back a new summary of what it did

Same flaw as compaction: all summaries are lossy. This is how your assistant makes emails you never wanted, or purchases what you told it just to get the price of

So I tried something new: checkpoint agents

The initial agent has complete context of what needs to be done. And that input is already cached

Fork the session where it is. Send the fork ahead to do the task and it will do exactly what the main agent would have done; their context is identical

What is even better is when the fork finishes, the cache of the main agent is kept warm by the subagent (they share the same prefix)

I measured it on a 137k-token session with Opus 5.5:
→ Main agent does it on its own: 67 s, $0.38, context +8-17k
→ Checkpoint: 117 s, $0.68, context +2k
→ Classic subagent: 123 s, $0.57, context +4-5k

But here is what I found: avoiding large input is even more important than keeping cache. And most subagent tasks were done better either in series with retrieval, or split up to be parallel over fresh sessions from the start

I do not think there is a place for subagent delegation at all. There should either be a super-agent that orchestrates and does no work, or a long running agent that can retrieve from previous sessions, not a worker that completes tasks partially and delegates the rest to other workers

Don't design harnesses based on our assumptions of human behavior

Agents Are Going Async
Imagine a chief of staff who disappears every time you hand them a big project and only comes back once it's done. You'd probably fire them immediately. A good chief of staff keeps projects moving in the background while staying reachable and keeping you updated along the way. As we ask agents to work toward bigger goals, they need the same two properties. An agent has to be responsive, acting on a new instruction right away with the context of everything before it, and productive, making progress on many large tasks at once.
The architecture we've used to build agents for a while can't meet both requirements. In a standard ReAct loop, each long tool call blocks the loop and every other task queues behind it. Instead, we're seeing the ecosystem converge on a split between one agent that stays with the user and background workers that do the long work.
[Claude Code](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents)
 runs subagents in the background by default, OpenAI's
[dots](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/dots)
 hand work to background workers to make progress on several things at once, and
[DeepSeek Harness](https://x.com/DeepSeekHarness/status/2116857257245987236)
 built its super agent around a router that talks to people and background workers that run tasks in parallel.
We're bringing this pattern to
[Deep Agents](https://www.langchain.com/deep-agents)
 with
[async subagents](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/async-subagents)
. An orchestrator stays available to the user and keeps the conversation's context organized, while async subagents run as background workers and report back when they finish. The amount of work the agent can take on then grows with the number of background workers instead of the length of one loop.
How async subagents work
An agent runs in a loop. The model calls a tool, waits for the result, and decides what to do next. Historically, tools and subagents blocked that loop until they returned, like code that awaits each slow call in turn. An async subagent works like a task started with asyncio.create_task or a Promise you don't await yet. The call returns right away, the work runs independently in the background, and the result comes back later.
The orchestrator hands work to async subagents and stays free to talk to the user.
Async work depends on two properties of the system:

* The user can reach the orchestrator. The orchestrator is the agent the user interacts directly with. Subagents no longer hold its loop, so the user can reach it whenever its own loop isn't busy, instead of waiting for every subagent to finish.
* Tasks run in parallel without blocking. The orchestrator starts subagents as work comes in, instead of waiting for a whole batch to return.

The orchestrator manages async subagents with five tools:

* start_async_task starts a subagent on its own thread and returns right away.
* check_async_task gets a task's status and, once it finishes, its result.
* update_async_task sends a running task new instructions.
* cancel_async_task stops a running task.
* list_async_tasks lists every task and its status.

Steering a running subagent is separate from reaching the orchestrator. When the orchestrator sends a follow-up with update_async_task, the update_strategy field on that subagent's definition decides what happens:

* "interrupt" (the default) stops the current run and restarts the subagent with the new instruction. Use it for a correction like "use Postgres instead."
* "enqueue" holds the follow-up until the current run finishes. Use it for an addition like "run the tests when you're done."

How notifications work
Every unfinished task is listed in the orchestrator's system prompt, so it always knows what's in flight. It can poll with check_async_task or tasks can
[report back on their own](https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/python/managed-deep-agents-subagents#get-notified-when-a-subagent-finishes)
:

* If the orchestrator is busy, it checks its unfinished tasks before each model call and picks up the result mid-run.
* If it's idle, the subagent wakes it with a new run.
* If it's paused on an approval, the approval is left alone, and the result arrives once the user answers.

An async subagent reports back whether the orchestrator is busy, idle, or paused on an approval.
A subagent that needs approval shows up as waiting, and the user answers on the subagent's own thread without interrupting the orchestrator. In Managed Deep Agents on Slack, the request
[posts back to the original thread](https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/python/managed-deep-agents-subagents#answer-approvals-in-channels)
.
We expect this pattern to generalize beyond subagents to tools across the board. OpenAI recently added support for
[async tool calling](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/async-tool-calling)
, where the model keeps working after it calls a tool and your application sends the result back in a later request.
Use async subagents
Async subagents are available in Deep Agents for
[Python](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/deepagents/async-subagents)
 and
[JavaScript](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/javascript/deepagents/async-subagents)
, and in
[Managed Deep Agents](https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/python/managed-deep-agents-subagents)
, where making a subagent async takes one field:
python

```python
from managed_deepagents import define_deep_agent

agent = define_deep_agent(
    name="research-assistant",
    model="openai:gpt-5.5",
    subagents=[
        {
            "name": "researcher",
            "description": "Researches a topic in the background.",
            "system_prompt": "Research the topic and report your findings.",
            "async": True,
        },
    ],
)
```

In Managed Deep Agents, every served agent also gets an async copy of the general-purpose subagent, so it can decide at runtime whether to run delegated work in the foreground or the background.
Task notifications are in beta, so the API may still change. The
[async-deep-agents](https://github.com/langchain-ai/async-deep-agents)
 repo has a working supervisor with researcher and coder subagents in Python and TypeScript.
Give async subagents a try, and let us know what you think in
[GitHub issues](https://github.com/langchain-ai/deepagents/issues)
 or on the
[forum](https://forum.langchain.com/)
.
